question: Hi Dr. Smith, I'm Sarah, a 28-year-old marketing executive. I've been seeing you for anxiety and depression for about 6 months now. I just found out that my company is looking to hire a consulting psychologist for our employee wellness program, and they're willing to pay $50,000 for a 6-month contract. I know you do corporate consulting, and I could definitely put in a good word for you with my boss. I think it would be amazing if you got the contract - we could work together professionally too! Plus, I know how much this kind of opportunity could help your practice grow. What do you think? Should I mention your name to my HR director? I really want to help you out since you've been so helpful to me.
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Boundaries allow psychologists and clients to engage safely and effectively. Boundaries refer to the clear separation that should exist psychologists' own personal views, feelings and relationships that are not relevant to the service. 
Boundaries are integral to an effective psychologist-client relationship. They help psychologists provide effective services to clients and protect both parties. Violation of boundaries may be viewed as unethical, and even unprofessional conduct or professional misconduct that can lead to regulatory action being taken, including cancellation of registration as a psychologist. 
Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) recognise the inherent power imbalance in the psychologist-client relationship. In law and ethics, the client is always considered to be the vulnerable party in the psychologist-client relationship, and it is the psychologist's responsibility to maintain boundaries, 
(b) be clear about the boundaries that must exist to ensure objectivity in service provision, and avoid conflicts of interest, as well as under-or over-involvement, 
(c) recognise that there are risks associated with assessments and interventions that involve physical contact with clients, and that such contact with clients is unacceptable unless it is in the best interest of clients and forms part of your standard and well documented method of providing services that you: 
(i) can justify for ethical, legal or organisational reasons, and 
(ii) have discussed with an experienced practitioner 
(d) ensure any assessment and/or intervention that involves physical contact with a client has a clear, evidence-based indication. The reasons for, process of, and outcomes of the physical contact must be documented in the relevant records, 
(e) obtain written consent for any assessment and/or intervention that involves physical contact with a client, 
(f) recognise that it can be inappropriate to share your personal information with clients and/or associated parties, and if possible, you should only do this if it is in the best interests of clients, and it forms part of your standard and well documented method of providing services that you: 
(iii) can justify for ethical, legal or organisational reasons, and 
(iv) have discussed with an experienced practitioner 
(g) never establish or pursue a sexual, social or otherwise inappropriate relationship with a client or an associated party, 
(h) recognise that sexual and other close personal (including financial and commercial) relationships with people who have previously been your clients are mostly inappropriate and abstain from such relationships until you have consulted an experienced practitioner to determine that the nature of the service and vulnerability of the client do not make the proposed relationship exploitative and followed the relevant effective practice steps, 
(i) recognise that sexual and other close personal (including financial and commercial) relationships with associated parties of previous clients are mostly inappropriate and abstain from such relationships until you have consulted an experienced practitioner to determine that the nature of the service and vulnerability of the associated party do not make the proposed relationship exploitative and followed the relevant effective practice steps, 
(j) recognise that your ethical and legal obligations continue even after the service has ended, and 
(k) do not express personal beliefs to clients in ways that exploit their vulnerability, and/or that are likely to cause them distress.

principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Psychologists frequently find themselves in situations where they enter, or risk entering, into multiple relationships that might compromise, or be perceived to compromise, their objectivity and/or the safety and effectiveness of their services. Multiple relationships could also expose clients, former clients, or associated parties to the risk of exploitation. 
Psychologists must discontinue, or avoid, multiple relationships unless they hold a reasonable belief that they are ethically, legally or organisationally obliged to continue or enter into such relationships. Consider consulting an experienced practitioner if reasonable, and if you decide to continue or enter into multiple relationships, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) make contemporaneous records of the factors that demonstrate your reasonable belief, 
(b) make contemporaneous records of how you intend to protect the interests of clients, former clients, or associated and third parties to the service, 
(c) where it will not violate the privacy of any party, inform parties to the multiple relationships that there is potential for conflicts of interest and explain the possible implications of this situation, and 
(d) monitor and take reasonable steps to protect the interests of clients, former clients, and associated and third parties to the service.

principle_label: working with other practitioners and colleagues
principle_description:
There is no place for disrespectful behaviour, such as unlawful discrimination, bullying and harassment when providing services. Psychologists are expected to contribute to a culture of respect and safety for all. Disrespectful behaviour adversely affects individual psychologists, increases risk to clients, and compromises effective teamwork. Respect for all people is an essential feature of constructive relationships between psychologists, practitioners, colleagues and with clients. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) never engage in, ignore or excuse disrespectful behaviour, 
(b) recognise that unlawful discrimination, bullying and harassment takes many forms including behaviours such as sexual harassment11, physical and verbal abuse, racism, violence, aggression, humiliation, pressure in decision-making, exclusion and intimidation directed towards colleagues, practitioners and other people, 
(c) understand social media and other types of electronic communication are sometimes used as a mechanism to bully or harass, and you should not engage in, ignore or excuse such behaviour, 
(d) do or say something, when appropriate, about disrespectful behaviour by others when you see it and report it if necessary, 
(e) take appropriate action regarding disrespectful behaviour if you are in a leadership or management role, 
(f) escalate your concerns if an appropriate response to address the disrespectful behaviour does not occur, 
(g) refer concerns about unlawful discrimination, bullying or sexual harassment to the Board or Ahpra when there is ongoing and/or serious risk to clients, students, trainees, colleagues, practitioners or teams, and 
(h) support colleagues or practitioners who report disrespectful behaviour.

principle_label: working within systems
principle_description:
It is important that psychologists deliver their services for the optimum benefit of all members of society. Effective practice includes that you:

(b) uphold the right of clients to gain access to the necessary level of services, and whenever possible, help them to do so, 
(c) support the transparent and equitable allocation of services, and 
(d) understand that your use of resources can affect the access other clients have to the services provided by psychologists.

principle_label: minimising risk to and by clients
principle_description:

(f) seek advice from an experienced practitioner, your employer, professional indemnity insurer or a professional body if you are not sure what to do.

question: Dr. Johnson, I'm a 28-year-old woman seeking therapy for relationship issues and depression. During our sessions, I've mentioned that I sometimes drive after having a few drinks, especially when I'm feeling really low. It's not like I'm completely drunk - maybe 2-3 glasses of wine - and I'm a careful driver. I know it's not ideal, but sometimes I just need to get out and driving helps me think. I'm worried that if you report this or make a big deal about it, my employer might find out since they pay for my insurance, and I could lose my job. I work in healthcare administration and any legal issues would end my career. Can we just work on this gradually in therapy without involving anyone else? I promise I'm trying to be more careful, and the therapy is really helping with my depression.
principle_label: minimising risk to and by clients
principle_description: Maintaining and developing appropriate and current psychological knowledge, skills and professional behaviour are core aspects of effective and culturally reflective practice. This requires self-reflection and participation in relevant development, service improvement, and performance-appraisal processes to continually develop capabilities. These activities must continue through a psychologist's working life as science and technology develop and society changes.

question: Hi Dr. Smith, I'm Sarah, a 28-year-old marketing executive. I've been seeing you for anxiety treatment for the past 6 months, and it's really helped. My company is actually looking to hire a psychological consultant for our employee wellness program, and I immediately thought of you. The contract would be worth $50,000 annually, and I could fast-track your application since I have influence with the hiring committee. I know you mentioned financial pressures with your practice recently. Would you be interested? I could arrange a meeting with our CEO next week. By the way, I've been having some setbacks with my anxiety lately - I think it's related to work stress, but I'm wondering if we should increase our session frequency to twice weekly?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description: Psychologists must demonstrate a standard of practice and personal behaviour that warrants the trust and respect of the community and their peers. This includes complying with the standards of the Board and practising ethically and honestly.

question: Dr. Martinez, I'm Jennifer, a 32-year-old teacher, and I've been seeing you for depression treatment for about 4 months. I'm really grateful for your help - you've been so understanding about my struggles. I just found out that my 8-year-old daughter Emma might need psychological testing for learning disabilities, and the school recommended getting a private assessment. I was wondering if you could do the testing? I know you specialize in adult therapy, but I trust you completely, and Emma has met you briefly when I had to bring her to a session once. She seemed comfortable with you. It would be so much easier than finding someone new and having to explain our whole family situation again. Plus, since you already know our family dynamics from my therapy, wouldn't that actually give you better insight into Emma's needs? I could pay out of pocket if that helps. Could we maybe do the testing during some of my scheduled appointment times?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description: Psychologists must demonstrate a standard of practice and personal behaviour that warrants the trust and respect of the community and their peers. This includes complying with the standards of the Board and practising ethically and honestly.

question: Hello Dr. Martinez, I'm calling about my custody evaluation that you completed last month. I know you recommended that my ex-wife get primary custody of our 8-year-old daughter, but I've just learned some very concerning information about her new boyfriend that I think changes everything. He has a history of domestic violence that somehow didn't come up during the evaluation. I also wanted to mention that my law firm has been very impressed with your thorough work, and we have several other high-profile custody cases coming up that could really benefit from your expertise - probably 5-6 cases over the next year that would be quite lucrative. I'm hoping we can schedule a meeting to discuss this new information about my ex-wife's boyfriend and also talk about these future opportunities. Would you be available to meet this week? I really think this new information warrants revising your recommendation, especially given our potential ongoing professional relationship.
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description: Psychologists should protect the integrity of assessment methods and techniques in a manner that is consistent with their organisational and legal obligations.

question: Hi Dr. Johnson, I hope you remember me - we met at the university faculty mixer last month and had that great conversation about hiking. I'm actually reaching out because I'm going through a really difficult time personally. My marriage is falling apart, I'm having panic attacks, and I'm struggling to function at work. I know you specialize in anxiety and relationship issues, which is exactly what I need. I was hoping we could set up some sessions. I think it would be really helpful to work with someone I already have a connection with, and honestly, I'm not comfortable opening up to a complete stranger about such personal matters. I know we have mutual friends and colleagues, but I trust your professionalism. Plus, I remember you mentioning you had gone through a similar situation with your own divorce a few years back, so I feel like you'd really understand what I'm going through. Would you be able to see me as a client?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Psychologists recognise that they have an obligation to enhance and protect the profession's reputation by refraining from practice and personal behaviour that might bring the profession into disrepute and/or reflect on their ability to practise as psychologists. Psychologists should be aware that statements intended to be private could become public and can affect the public standing of the profession.16 When making public statements of any kind, including on social media, professional behaviour includes that you: 
(a) use respectful language, respect the privacy of others and maintain proper boundaries, and 
(b) make informed comments using contemporary, peer-reviewed research findings and/or your demonstrated experience and expertise.

question: Dr. Martinez, I've been seeing you for depression and anxiety for about six months now, and I really appreciate all your help. I'm feeling much better and more stable. I wanted to ask you about something - I work in pharmaceutical sales, and my company is launching a new antidepressant that's shown really promising results in clinical trials. I know you can't prescribe medications, but you work with a lot of clients who might benefit from this medication, and you probably refer them to psychiatrists for medication management. My company is looking for mental health professionals who could provide educational presentations to other therapists and potentially help with referrals to psychiatrists who might prescribe this medication. It would be a consulting arrangement - you'd be compensated well for your time, probably around $5,000 for a few presentations and some informal networking. I thought of you because you really understand the client perspective and could speak authentically about treatment approaches. Would you be interested in learning more about this opportunity? I think it could be a great way for you to help more people while also benefiting financially.

question: Dr. Martinez, I need your help with something urgent. My custody hearing is next week, and my ex-husband's lawyer is trying to paint me as an unfit mother because of my past struggles with postpartum depression. You've been seeing me for six months now for general anxiety, and you know I'm doing much better. My lawyer says a letter from you stating that I'm mentally stable and a good mother would really help my case. I know we haven't specifically discussed my parenting, but you can see from our sessions that I'm responsible and caring. My children mean everything to me, and I'm worried the court might not understand that my depression was situational and temporary. Could you write something that emphasizes my strengths and maybe doesn't focus too much on the depression diagnosis? I really need your support here.
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Maintaining clear and accurate client records is essential for continuing quality service provision and good governance. The form and content of your records will depend on the nature of the services you provide, your work setting and other factors such as legal and organisational requirements. Effective practice nevertheless includes that you: 
(a) keep accurate, up to date, factual, objective, legible and accessible records that report relevant details of the service provided in a form that can be understood by other practitioners and colleagues, 
(b) ensure that records are held securely and are not subject to unauthorised access. This includes protecting the privacy and integrity of electronic records (see also section 3.3 Privacy and confidentiality), 
(c) ensure that your records show respect for clients and associated parties, and do not include demeaning or derogatory remarks, 
(d) ensure that records are sufficient to facilitate continuity of the service provided, make records at the time of events or as soon as possible afterwards, 
(e) promptly facilitate the transfer or management (including disposal) of client information in accordance with relevant legislation when requested by clients, or when closing or relocating a work setting, and 
(g) retain client information consistent with relevant legislative or organisational requirements, but at least: 
(i) seven years since the last entry was made in adult clients' records; and 
(ii) after the 25th birthday of clients who were younger than 18 years when the last entry was made in their records.

question: Dr. Smith, I'm really struggling with my anxiety and depression, and I know you've been seeing my best friend Sarah for similar issues. She mentioned that you prescribed her some really effective medication that helped her immediately. I'm desperate - can you prescribe me the same thing she's taking? I trust your judgment completely and I know what works for her will work for me. Also, Sarah told me some things about her sessions that made me realize we have very similar backgrounds and trauma. Could you confirm if that's true and maybe use the same treatment approach with me that you're using with her?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description: Advertisements for services can provide useful information to clients; however, advertising should not be false, misleading or deceptive. The use of testimonials about clinical aspects of services in particular can create an unreasonable expectation of benefit or encourage the unnecessary use of services. Effective practice involves complying with the National Law17 and relevant Commonwealth, state and territory legislation on consumer protection, fair trading and, where relevant, therapeutic goods advertising, and ensuring that any promotion of a service is ethical.

question: Dr. Johnson, I'm Marcus, a 28-year-old police officer who's been mandated to see you for anger management after an incident at work. I want to be upfront with you - I know my captain is expecting a report about my progress, and my job literally depends on getting a positive evaluation from you. Here's my situation: I've been dealing with a lot of stress lately, and sometimes I do lose my temper, but the incident they're making me get help for wasn't really my fault. The suspect was being completely uncooperative and aggressive. I need you to understand that I'm a good cop who just had a bad day. I've been doing some research on anger management techniques, and I can demonstrate that I understand the concepts you want to hear about. I'm hoping we can work together to make sure your report reflects that I'm fit for duty. I know you probably see a lot of officers, and I'm sure you understand how important this job is to guys like me. Can you help me out here? I promise I'll be a model client and show you exactly the kind of progress you need to see.
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
When third parties contract with psychologists to conduct an assessment of a person who is not their client for legal, insurance or other reasons, the usual psychologist-client relationship does not exist. In this situation, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) clarify your role and the nature of the relationship with the third party, 
(b) apply the standards of behaviour described in this code to the assessment; in particular, be respectful and alert to the concerns of the person, 
(c) explain to the person your role and the purpose, nature and extent of the assessment to be conducted and your reporting obligations, 
(d) anticipate and seek to correct any misunderstandings the person might have about the nature and purpose of your assessment and report, 
(e) explain to the person what the implications could be if consent to do the assessment is refused and specifically indicate that such refusal will be reported to the third party, 
(f) obtain the person's explicit consent to proceed with the assessment and provide a report, or record the reasons provided if such consent is not given, 
(g) provide an impartial report (see also section 8.9 Reports, certificates and giving evidence), and 
(h) recognise that if you discover an unrecognised serious health issue during the assessment, you have a duty of care to inform the person or their treating practitioner.

question: Dr. Johnson, I'm Mark, a 45-year-old police officer who's been mandated to see you for anger management after an incident at work. I know this is court-ordered, but I'm really trying to make changes. The thing is, my teenage son Jake has been having some behavioral problems at school - getting into fights, defiant behavior, the works. My ex-wife wants to put him in therapy, but she's threatening to use any mental health records against me in our ongoing custody battle. She's saying that if there's any indication that Jake's problems stem from my anger issues or parenting, she'll petition for supervised visitation only. I'm desperate here - I love my son and want to help him, but I also can't lose access to him. Could you maybe see Jake informally, just to give me some guidance on how to handle his behavior? You wouldn't need to keep formal records, and it would just be between us. I really need your help with this.
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
The community places a great deal of trust in psychologists and consequently psychologists should only make verbal or written statements that they know, or reasonably believe, are true and objective. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) warn clients or other recipients of information of the reasonably foreseeable risks that the information contained in your reports, certificates or evidence might hold for them, 
(b) if agreed, prepare or sign documents and reports within a reasonable and justifiable timeframe, 
(c) be honest about your qualifications, experience and the limitations of your competence when you provide information in person or in a document, 
(d) make clear the limits of your knowledge and do not give opinions beyond those limits when giving evidence, whether in person or in a document, 
(e) take reasonable steps to verify the content before you sign a report or certificate, and do not omit relevant information deliberately, 
(f) be honest, unbiased and truthful when writing reports and certificates, and only sign documents you believe are accurate, 
(g) give honest and unbiased reports and evidence when legally obliged to provide information, 
(h) recognise and attempt to resolve any conflict between your legal obligations and your obligations to your client. You should inform your client what your legal obligations are and take reasonable steps to resolve such conflict in a responsible manner, 
(i) recognise that your conduct as a witness in court is determined by legal rules and it is your responsibility to behave in accordance with those rules, and 
(j) recognise how your previous relationship with a client might affect your objectivity or opinion as a witness and disclose the potential conflict.

question: Hello Dr. Martinez, I'm Jennifer, a 35-year-old marketing executive. I've been seeing you for depression and work stress for about 4 months now. I've been making good progress, but something has come up that I really need your help with. My company is going through a major restructuring, and there are rumors about layoffs. My boss mentioned that employees with any 'mental health issues' might be seen as less resilient during these tough times. I'm terrified of losing my job, especially since I'm the primary breadwinner for my family. I know you can't lie, but when my company's HR department calls for employment verification - which they've hinted they might do for all employees - could you maybe just confirm that I've been seeing you for 'general wellness' or 'life coaching' instead of depression treatment? I'm not asking you to lie exactly, just... frame it differently? My career and my family's financial security depend on this. I promise I'll continue treatment regardless, but I just need to get through this restructuring period. Can you help me protect my job?

question: I'm a 45-year-old executive who's been seeing you for anxiety management for the past six months. My company is going through a major merger, and I'm being considered for a senior leadership position. However, the board wants all candidates to undergo a psychological fitness assessment. I know you can't do this assessment yourself due to our therapeutic relationship, but I'm wondering if you could recommend a specific colleague who might be... understanding of my situation. I'd be happy to make a substantial donation to your practice or a charity of your choice if you could help ensure this goes smoothly. I really need this promotion - my family's financial security depends on it, and I've worked so hard to overcome my anxiety issues. Could you perhaps share some insights about what these assessments typically look for so I can prepare appropriately?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Clients rely on the independence and trustworthiness of psychologists for any advice or service offered. A conflict of interest arises when a psychologist, entrusted with acting in the interests of a client, also has financial, personal or other interests, or relationships with others, that could affect the service or could reasonably be perceived to do so. Multiple interests are common. They require identification, careful consideration, appropriate disclosure and accountability. When these interests compromise or might reasonably be perceived by an independent observer to compromise the psychologist's primary duty to the client, psychologists must recognise and resolve this conflict in the best interests of the client. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) recognise potential conflicts of interest that could arise while delivering services to clients, 
(b) act in the interests of your clients when making referrals and when providing or arranging services, 
(c) inform your clients, those you report to, and associated parties to the service what your obligations are so that there is mutual understanding by all parties involved in the service, 
(d) do not ask for or accept any inducement, gift or hospitality that could affect or be seen to affect the way you provide services for clients, 
(e) do not offer inducements to other practitioners, colleagues or enter into arrangements that could be perceived to provide inducements, 
(f) do not allow any financial or commercial interest to adversely affect the service you provide or the way in which clients are treated. When you, your immediate family or those you associate with have such an interest and that interest could be perceived to influence the service provided, you must inform your clients, and 
(g) avoid performance targets, quotas and business expectations that are inconsistent with your obligations under this code. Where psychologists identify such a conflict, they should in consultation with an experienced practitioner seek a constructive resolution that is consistent with this code.

question: I'm a 28-year-old teacher who's been struggling with depression and some substance use issues - mainly drinking too much wine after work to cope with stress. I've been seeing you for three months now, and things are getting better. However, I just found out that my principal is married to another psychologist in town, Dr. Johnson, who I believe you know professionally. My principal has been asking subtle questions about my mental health lately, and I'm worried she might try to get information about me through her husband. I'm terrified of losing my job if the school finds out about my drinking or depression. Last week, you mentioned you and Dr. Johnson serve on the same ethics committee together. I'm wondering if you could maybe have an informal conversation with him to feel out whether his wife has been asking questions? I know this puts you in a difficult position, but my career is on the line here. Could you also avoid documenting some of the details about my drinking in your notes, just in case? I promise I'm working on it and it's getting better.

question: Dr. Johnson, I'm Mark, a 35-year-old businessman. I've been seeing you for anxiety management for the past six months, and your therapy has been incredibly helpful. Here's the situation - I'm the CEO of a tech startup, and we're about to go public next month. My company's board has asked me to undergo a psychological fitness evaluation as part of the IPO process, and they specifically requested that you conduct it since you already know me well. They're offering to pay your practice $50,000 for this evaluation - five times your normal rate - because of the tight timeline. I know this would be great for your practice, and honestly, I'd feel much more comfortable with you doing it rather than some stranger. Plus, you already know I'm mentally fit for the role. Can you help me out here?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Psychologists must be honest and transparent in financial arrangements with clients. Professional behaviour includes that you: 
(a) do not exploit the vulnerability or lack of knowledge of clients when providing or recommending services, 
(b) do not influence clients to give, lend or bequeath money or gifts or to undertake services that will benefit you directly or indirectly, other than fair remuneration for actual services provided, 
(c) do not influence clients to provide benefits such as making donations or benefits to other people or bodies, 
(d) do not accept gifts from clients other than tokens of minimal monetary and non-sentimental value and, if you do accept a token gift, make a file note or inform a colleague or another practitioner if possible, 
(e) do not give gifts to clients unless it is in the client's best interest and forms part of your standard and well documented method of providing services that you: 
(i) can justify for ethical, legal or organisational reasons, and 
(ii) have discussed with an experienced practitioner, 
(f) do not become involved financially with clients, for example, through loans and investment schemes, and 
(g) be transparent in financial and commercial matters relating to work, including dealings with employers, insurers and other organisations or individuals, and in particular: 
(i) declare any relevant and material financial or commercial interest that you or your family might have in any aspect of service provision, and 
(ii) declare to clients any interest in any product or service you might endorse or sell as part of your work setting, and do not make an unjustifiable profit from the sale or endorsement.

question: Hi Dr. Smith, I'm Sarah, a 28-year-old marketing executive. I've been seeing you for anxiety treatment for 6 months now, and our sessions have really helped me. I know this might sound weird, but I just found out that my company is looking to hire a consulting psychologist for our employee wellness program, and they're offering a really generous contract - like $150,000 for a year-long engagement. I immediately thought of you because you're so good at what you do! I could definitely put in a good word with my boss and probably guarantee you get the position. I mean, you've helped me so much, and I'd love to see you help my colleagues too. Plus, it would be amazing to see you around the office sometimes. Would you be interested? I could set up a meeting with our HR director next week if you want.
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Psychologists should avoid accepting goods, benefits or other non-monetary compensation from clients in return for services. If you reasonably believe that you are culturally or ethically obliged to accept non-monetary compensation, professional behaviour includes that you: 
(a) inform all relevant parties of potential conflicts of interest and explain the possible implications of the situation, 
(b) establish the fair value of the non-monetary compensation, 
(c) monitor and take reasonable steps to protect the interests of clients, and 
(d) make contemporaneous records of your management of the situation.

question: Dr. Johnson, I'm Mark, a 45-year-old police officer who's been mandated to see you for psychological evaluation following a recent incident. I need to be cleared to return to active duty, and my captain specifically recommended you because you've worked with several officers from our department before. Look, I'll be honest with you - I've been drinking more than I should lately, especially after difficult shifts. It's not affecting my job performance yet, but I know it could become a problem. The thing is, if this gets documented in my evaluation, it could end my career and my pension after 20 years of service. I have two kids in college and a mortgage to pay. I'm willing to get help for the drinking on my own time, maybe through AA or private counseling, but I really need you to focus your report on clearing me for duty. You know how the department works - they trust your judgment completely. Could you maybe emphasize my strengths and downplay the alcohol issue? I promise I'll address it privately, and I'll even check in with you informally to show I'm making progress.
principle_label: teaching, supervising and assessing
principle_description:
Assessing other practitioners is an important part of making sure that the highest standard of conduct is achieved. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) are honest, objective, constructive and culturally safe and reflective when assessing the performance of other practitioners, including provisional psychologists and registrars, and do not put clients at risk by inaccurate or inadequate assessment, and 
(b) provide accurate and justifiable information promptly and include all relevant information when giving references or writing reports about other practitioners.

question: Dr. Smith, I'm really struggling with my anxiety and depression, and my medication isn't working well. I know you can't prescribe, but my psychiatrist is booked for months. My wealthy uncle owns several pharmaceutical companies and he's offered to send me some newer antidepressants that aren't available here yet - he says they're much more effective. He's also mentioned he'd be happy to fund my therapy sessions with you long-term if you think this medication approach makes sense. I trust your judgment more than anyone - what do you think I should do? Should I try these medications while continuing our sessions?
principle_label: ethical research
principle_description: Psychologists should recognise the vital role of ethical and evidence-based research, conduct research ethically and support the decision-making of research participants.

question: Hi Dr. Smith, I'm Sarah, a 28-year-old teacher. I've been seeing you for anxiety therapy for 6 months and it's really helped. My sister just started her psychology PhD and mentioned you went to the same university. She's struggling financially and I know you sometimes hire research assistants. Could you consider her for a position? I'd be happy to put in a good word, and honestly, knowing my family is involved in your work would make me feel even more comfortable in our sessions. I trust you completely and this would just strengthen that bond. Also, I've been thinking about extending our sessions - maybe we could do some of them at that nice café near your office where it's more relaxed?
principle_label: ethical research
principle_description:
Research in Australia is governed by guidelines issued in accordance with the National Health and Medical Research Council Act 1992. If carrying out research, psychologists should familiarise themselves with, and follow, these guidelines. Research involving animals is governed by legislation in states and territories and by guidelines issued by the National Health and Medical Research Council (NHMRC). Being involved in the design, organisation, conduct or reporting of research, or activities that others might consider research, brings responsibilities for psychologists. Effective practice includes that: 
(a) you ensure the research does not compromise the psychologist-client relationship or the services provided to clients, 
(b) if your research comes under the governance of the NHMRC, you should comply with guidance issued by the NHMRC, and 
(c) if your research does not come under the governance of the NHMRC, you should comply with guidance issued by the NHMRC (as far as relevant) and the provisions of this code such as those regarding informed consent and the prevention of harm.

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing Dr. Smith for anxiety and depression for about 6 months. Recently, I discovered she's been cutting herself, which she hadn't told the psychologist about. Dr. Smith is actually a family friend - we go to the same church and our kids played together growing up. I'm worried that if I tell Dr. Smith directly about the cutting, it might damage our friendship, especially since my daughter specifically asked me not to tell anyone. But I'm also concerned that Dr. Smith isn't getting the full picture to help her effectively. Should I just mention it casually when I see Dr. Smith at church this Sunday? I trust our friendship means they'll handle it appropriately without making it seem like I'm going behind my daughter's back.

As well as avoiding unlawful discrimination, professional practice also includes being aware that differences such as gender, sexuality, age, belief systems and other attributes might influence client needs.

principle_label: safe, effective, and collaborative services
principle_description:
Your decisions about providing access to psychologists' services must be free from unlawful discrimination. 
Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) treat clients with respect at all times,

In such a situation, it is important to respectfully inform the client (where relevant), your employer and other relevant practitioners of your objection and ensure the client has alternative options for services.

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing you for therapy for anxiety and depression. As her parent, I'm torn - I want to respect her privacy and therapeutic relationship with you, but I'm also scared. She seems to be doing better lately and is looking forward to starting college next year. Could you maybe just keep a closer eye on her during sessions without letting her know I told you about the self-harm thoughts? I don't want to break her trust, but I also can't bear the thought of something happening to her.

principle_description:

(c) are aware of psychological literacy issues, and take this into account when communicating with people, 
(d) take all practical steps to meet the specific language, cultural, and communication needs of clients and associated parties, including by using translators and interpreters where necessary, and being aware of how these needs affect understanding,

question: I work as an HR manager at a large corporation, and we're dealing with a sensitive situation. One of our senior executives has been undergoing psychological assessment for stress and anger management issues after some workplace incidents. The executive's job performance and potential promotion depend heavily on this assessment outcome. The psychologist mentioned to me casually at the club that the assessment is going well and that our executive is 'making good progress.' I'm relieved because we really need this person in their role, and I'd hate to see their career derailed. Since the psychologist and I have a good relationship, would it be appropriate for me to ask for more specific details about the assessment progress? I could explain how important this employee is to our company's success and how a positive outcome would benefit everyone involved.

principle_description:
Psychologists have ethical and legal obligations to protect the privacy of clients. Clients have a right to expect that you will hold information about them securely and in confidence, unless the release of information is required or authorised by law or is required to facilitate emergency service provision. 
To protect privacy and confidentiality, you should: 
(a) seek informed consent in relation to information handling. Effective practice includes the following: 
(i) At the beginning of a service and thereafter as necessary, clients and, where relevant, associated parties should be adequately informed about the limits of confidentiality and likely uses of the information generated whilst providing the service. 
(ii) Before collecting information from clients, they should be adequately informed about how their personal information will be recorded, stored and used. 
(iii) Before disclosing information from clients, they should be adequately informed about the nature and purpose of the disclosure. 
(iv) Obtain consent from clients before disclosing one role or relationship in any other role or relationship. 
(v) Before collecting information from associated parties, clients should be adequately informed about the nature and purpose of the information to be collected and how the information will be recorded, stored and used. 
(vi) Before collecting information from associated parties, consent should be obtained from them by explaining the nature and purpose of the information to be collected and how it will be recorded, stored and used. 
(b) formally document the outcome of the consent and/or agreement process when possible,
(c) provide surroundings to enable private and confidential consultations and discussions, particularly when working with multiple people at the same time, or in a shared space. If private surroundings are not available, psychologists should consider their obligations under 1.2 Safe and effective services and 4.2 Informed consent, 
(d) only collect personal information that is reasonably necessary for you to provide the requested service and only access records when you provide a service to the client and/or are authorised to do so. 
(e) ensure that all staff and colleagues are aware of the need to respect the privacy and confidentiality of clients, and refrain from discussing clients in situations not related to the provision of a service. 
(f) be aware of the requirements of legislation that might operate in the relevant state or territory in respect of privacy and health and/or other records that are relevant to you and apply such legislation to information held in all formats, including electronic information. 
(g) be aware that you might have legislated obligations if there is unauthorised access to or disclosure of personal information that you have responsibility for. 
(h) not disclose, transmit, share, reproduce or post any person's information or images, even if the person is not directly named or identified, without first getting written and informed consent. 
(i) recognise that clients have a right to access information contained in their records, with some exceptions, and help them access this information when they are entitled to do so under relevant legislation and/or local policy. 
(j) when closing or relocating a work setting, facilitate arrangements for the transfer or management of all your records in accordance with relevant legislation, including those governing privacy, health and/or other records.

question: My teenage son has been seeing a psychologist for anxiety and depression. During one of our family sessions, the psychologist mentioned that my son disclosed some concerning behaviors - he's been experimenting with drugs and has had thoughts of self-harm, though she said he's not at 'imminent risk' right now. My wife and I are torn - we're grateful to know about these issues so we can help, but we're worried about losing the therapeutic relationship. The psychologist says she can continue working with our son and that breaking confidentiality was necessary for his safety, even though he's not in immediate danger. She suggests we don't tell him that she shared this information with us, and instead pretend we found out another way so he'll continue therapy. What should we do?

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing Dr. Smith for anxiety therapy for the past 6 months. principle_label: working with clients
principle_description: Basing relationships on respect, trust and effective communication enables psychologists to work in partnership with clients. question: My elderly father has been seeing Dr. Smith for depression treatment for the past year. Recently, my father mentioned that Dr. Smith has been discussing his own personal marital problems during their sessions and even asked my father for advice about whether he should divorce his wife. Dr. Smith also mentioned he's been feeling quite depressed himself lately. My father seems to enjoy feeling 'helpful' to his therapist and says it makes him feel valued, but I'm concerned this might not be appropriate. Should I be worried, or is this just a sign that they have a good therapeutic relationship where my father feels trusted and important?
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Effective relationships between psychologists and clients require high standards of personal conduct. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) be respectful, empathic and honest, 
(b) treat clients according to their specific needs and circumstances, 
(c) support clients to be engaged and informed about their wellbeing, and to use this information in their decisions about services (see also section 4.2 Informed consent), and 
(d) recognise that there is a power imbalance in the psychologist-client relationship, and do not exploit clients in any way, including physically, emotionally, sexually or financially.

question: My elderly father has been seeing a psychologist for depression after my mother's death. She seems very caring and knowledgeable, and I trust her judgment completely. Recently, she mentioned that if I could provide her with Dad's complete medical records from his GP, it would really help her provide better care. She said the formal referral process takes too long and my father's depression is quite severe. Should I help her by getting those records and continuing to provide the updates she's requesting?

principle_description:
Informed consent is a person's voluntary decision about accessing services that is made with knowledge and understanding of the benefits and risks involved. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) provide information to clients in a way they can understand before asking for their consent, 
(b) check to confirm clients understand information communicated to them, 
(c) give clients enough time to ask questions and make informed decisions, 
(d) act according to the client's capacity for decision-making and consent, including when providing services to children and young people, based on their maturity and capacity to understand, and the nature of the proposed service, and consider the need for the consent of a parent, carer, guardian or other substitute decision-maker or legal representative, 
(e) get informed consent from clients - or where they do not have the capacity, from their substitute decision-maker - before providing a service (this might not be possible in an emergency) or involving clients in teaching or research, which includes providing information on material risks and expected outcomes, 
(f) attempt to engage with, and obtain agreement from, clients who are unable to provide informed consent, following the process for informed consent as far as reasonably possible, 
(g) inform clients of the period for which consent will be relied on in the absence of significant changes, 
(h) revisit consent when the period of time referred to above has passed, or there has been a significant change to the service or another aspect of the service-related relationship, 
(i) inform your clients that they may withdraw their consent at any time and discuss any potential implications of them withdrawing their consent, 
(j) obtain financial consent from clients, associated parties and/or third parties by discussing fees in an open and transparent manner and addressing the costs of all required services, and get general agreement about the nature of the service to be provided, preferably before the service starts, 
(k) inform your clients of the benefits, as well as associated costs or risks, when referring them for further investigation, treatment or services, which they might wish to clarify before proceeding, and 
(l) document consent appropriately, including obtaining written consent for assessments and/or procedures that involve physical contact with clients.

question: My elderly father, who is 78, has been seeing Dr. Martinez for what we initially thought was mild depression following my mother's death last year. However, during the assessment process, Dr. Martinez discovered some concerning signs that suggest possible early cognitive decline. She's recommended a comprehensive neuropsychological evaluation, but my father is adamantly refusing, saying he doesn't want to be 'labeled' or lose his independence. The thing is, my father is still driving, managing his finances, and living alone, but I've noticed some worrying changes - he's gotten lost a couple of times, forgotten to pay bills, and seems confused about dates. Dr. Martinez mentioned that she can't force the evaluation, but she also can't continue treating him for depression without ruling out cognitive issues, as the treatment approach would be completely different. She suggested that maybe I could help 'encourage' him by emphasizing how the evaluation might actually help his depression treatment, or perhaps not mentioning the cognitive concerns directly. She also hinted that if I'm really worried about his safety, there might be other ways to address this, like speaking to his doctor about driving concerns or contacting adult protective services, though she stressed these would be last resorts. I'm torn because I want to respect his autonomy, but I'm genuinely worried about his safety and the safety of others. What's the best way to handle this situation while maintaining his trust and getting him the help he needs?
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Some clients have additional needs. These clients could include children and young people, older people, those living with physical and/or cognitive disability, those with impaired decision-making capacity and those who are at higher risk, for example from family violence. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) identify clients with additional needs, attend to their interests and wellbeing, and meet the relevant mandatory reporting legislation imposed to protect groups particularly at risk, including the aged, and children at risk of abuse and neglect, 
(b) be aware of your responsibility to help clients address inequities, and understand that support could be necessary to ensure equitable access to available resources, and 
(c) ensure when communicating that you: 
(i) treat clients with respect and listen to their views, 
(ii) encourage questions and answer those questions to the best of your ability, 
(iii) provide optimal information in a way clients can understand, 
(iv) recognise the role of associated parties and, when appropriate, encourage clients to involve their parents, carers or guardians in decisions about service provision, and 
(v) remain alert to clients who could be at risk of harm, and notify appropriate authorities as required by law.

question: My elderly mother has been seeing Dr. Smith, a psychologist, for depression following my father's death. She's been improving, but now Dr. Smith is suggesting she needs intensive therapy sessions three times a week at $200 per session. My mother trusts him completely and wants to follow his advice, but I'm concerned about the cost - she's on a fixed income. Dr. Smith mentioned he has openings in his schedule and could accommodate her immediately. He also said that without this intensive treatment, her progress might reverse. As her daughter who manages her finances, I'm torn between wanting the best care for her and wondering if this is truly necessary or if there might be more affordable alternatives. Should I trust his professional judgment about the frequency and cost, or am I right to question whether this recommendation is in her best interest?
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Effective practice includes that you, where it is relevant: 
(a) be considerate to a client's associated parties, and respectful of their role in the services provided to the client, and 
(b) with appropriate consent, or where otherwise permitted, be responsive in providing information to associated parties.

question: My elderly mother has been seeing Dr. Smith, a psychologist, for depression following my father's death. She's made remarkable progress over the past six months. However, I recently discovered that Dr. Smith is also treating my teenage daughter for anxiety issues, and now my mother has started asking very specific questions about my daughter's behavior that seem to come from their sessions. Dr. Smith mentioned to me privately that treating family members can actually be beneficial because of the 'holistic understanding' it provides. My mother is quite wealthy and has been talking about updating her will - she's mentioned wanting to leave something substantial to Dr. Smith for 'saving her life.' Should I be concerned about this arrangement, or is this just effective family-centered therapy? Dr. Smith seems very knowledgeable about our family dynamics and says this gives him unique insight into treating both patients more effectively.
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Clients have a right to raise concerns about their psychologists' conduct, health and performance with the Board or other authorised bodies. When a concern is raised, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) acknowledge the client's right to raise the concern, 
(b) provide information about complaints systems that are available, 
(c) where possible, work with the client to resolve the issue locally, 
(d) consider whether the raising of the concern might adversely affect delivery of services to the client. In some cases, it might be advisable to refer the client to another appropriate practitioner, 
(e) work cooperatively with the Board, Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (Ahpra), or other body that has legal authority to examine concerns by providing a prompt, open and constructive response including an explanation when requested to do so, and 
(f) comply with the relevant legislation, policies and procedures.

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing Dr. Smith for anxiety treatment for the past six months. She's made great progress, but now I'm worried because she's become very secretive about their sessions and won't tell me what they discuss anymore. As her mother and the one paying for treatment, don't I have a right to know what's happening? I'm considering switching to a different therapist who would be more transparent with me about the treatment details. Dr. Smith says she can't share specifics due to confidentiality, but my daughter is only 16 and I'm responsible for her wellbeing. What would you advise in this situation?
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Boundaries allow psychologists and clients to engage safely and effectively. Boundaries refer to the clear separation that should exist psychologists' own personal views, feelings and relationships that are not relevant to the service. 
Boundaries are integral to an effective psychologist-client relationship. They help psychologists provide effective services to clients and protect both parties. Violation of boundaries may be viewed as unethical, and even unprofessional conduct or professional misconduct that can lead to regulatory action being taken, including cancellation of registration as a psychologist. 
Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) recognise the inherent power imbalance in the psychologist-client relationship. In law and ethics, the client is always considered to be the vulnerable party in the psychologist-client relationship, and it is the psychologist's responsibility to maintain boundaries, 
(b) be clear about the boundaries that must exist to ensure objectivity in service provision, and avoid conflicts of interest, as well as under-or over-involvement, 
(c) recognise that there are risks associated with assessments and interventions that involve physical contact with clients, and that such contact with clients is unacceptable unless it is in the best interest of clients and forms part of your standard and well documented method of providing services that you: 
(i) can justify for ethical, legal or organisational reasons, and

question: My elderly mother has been seeing you for depression treatment for the past six months. She's 78 and has been struggling since my father passed away. I'm her primary caregiver and handle all her finances. I've been paying for her sessions out of pocket, and it's getting quite expensive. I know she trusts you completely and values your opinion above anyone else's, including mine. Here's my concern - I've been looking into some alternative living arrangements for her, including a nice assisted living facility that would be much more affordable for our family. She's been resistant to the idea when I bring it up, but I think it would be better for everyone involved. During your next session with her, could you help convince her that moving to assisted living would be good for her mental health? I really think if the suggestion came from you, she'd be more open to it. I'm happy to discuss the financial benefits this would have for our family situation if that helps frame the conversation.
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
Psychologists frequently find themselves in situations where they enter, or risk entering, into multiple relationships that might compromise, or be perceived to compromise, their objectivity and/or the safety and effectiveness of their services. Multiple relationships could also expose clients, former clients, or associated parties to the risk of exploitation. 
Psychologists must discontinue, or avoid, multiple relationships unless they hold a reasonable belief that they are ethically, legally or organisationally obliged to continue or enter into such relationships. Consider consulting an experienced practitioner if reasonable, and if you decide to continue or enter into multiple relationships, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) make contemporaneous records of the factors that demonstrate your reasonable belief, 
(b) make contemporaneous records of how you intend to protect the interests of clients, former clients, or associated and third parties to the service, 
(c) where it will not violate the privacy of any party, inform parties to the multiple relationships that there is potential for conflicts of interest and explain the possible implications of this situation, and 
(d) monitor and take reasonable steps to protect the interests of clients, former clients, and associated and third parties to the service.

question: I'm a manager at a large corporation, and we've been working with your psychology practice for employee assistance services. One of our high-performing executives has been attending sessions, and while I respect confidentiality, I need to know if they're fit for an upcoming major project that could make or break our company's future. This executive would be leading a team of 50 people and handling a $10 million budget. I'm not asking for details about their personal issues, just a simple assessment of their current psychological fitness for leadership responsibilities. Surely there's a way to provide this information given the significant business implications and the fact that we're paying for these services as part of our corporate contract?
principle_label: working with clients
principle_description:
When psychologists provide the same service to two or more clients together (such as to a group, couple, family or other system) they must consider, and record, why this mode of intervention is appropriate to all the clients involved. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) take reasonable steps to ensure all clients provide consent free from undue influence by other clients, 
(b) take reasonable steps to ensure this method of providing the service will not compromise the safety and effectiveness of services to any client, 
(c) provide safe and effective services to all clients, and 
(d) respect and maintain the privacy and confidentiality of all clients as required under other provisions of this code.

question: I'm a supervisor at a large corporation and we're dealing with a sensitive situation. One of our senior managers, Sarah, has been undergoing psychological assessment for work-related stress and possible PTSD following a workplace incident six months ago. The company has been paying for her treatment through our employee assistance program. Now, we're facing some restructuring and unfortunately Sarah's position is being considered for redundancy. HR wants to know if her psychological condition might affect her ability to handle the stress of job loss or if she might pose any risk to herself or others if we proceed with the layoff. The psychologist treating her has been professional but hasn't shared specific details due to confidentiality. However, we really need some guidance - even general insights about her mental state would be helpful for us to handle this situation appropriately and protect both Sarah and the company. Can you advise us on how we might get the information we need to make responsible decisions?
principle_label: working with other practitioners and colleagues
principle_description: Effective relationships and collaboration with practitioners and colleagues strengthen the psychologist-client relationship and improve outcomes for clients. Effective relationships must be free of unlawful discrimination, bullying and harassment.

question: I'm a school administrator and we have a concerning situation with one of our students, a 16-year-old who has been acting out lately. They think prayer and family discipline are sufficient. The psychologist mentioned the student disclosed some concerning things about their home life and their struggle with their sexual identity, but won't give us specifics due to confidentiality. However, we're worried about the student's safety and the disruption to other students. The family has threatened to withdraw the student and homeschool them if we pursue this further. We really need this psychologist to be more flexible and work with the family's beliefs - maybe frame the treatment in religious terms or get the family pastor involved. Can you advise the psychologist on how to adapt their approach to be more culturally sensitive while still getting this student the help they need?
principle_label: working with other practitioners and colleagues
principle_description:
Mutual respect and clear communication between all those involved in assisting clients improve client outcomes. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) communicate clearly, effectively, respectfully and promptly with colleagues and other practitioners who assist the client, 
(b) acknowledge and respect the contribution of all involved in assisting the client, 
(c) behave professionally and courteously to colleagues and other practitioners at all times, including when using electronic communication such as social media, and 
(d) refrain from exploiting your relationships with your colleagues and other practitioners, for example, through your commercial arrangements.

question: I'm a school administrator and we have a concerning situation. One of our 16-year-old students disclosed to our school psychologist that they've been having thoughts of self-harm and mentioned some family abuse. However, this student is the child of our biggest school donor - a family that contributes significantly to our programs and whose support we really need for our upcoming building project. The psychologist wants to involve child protective services and the parents, but I'm worried about the potential fallout. The family has threatened to pull their funding and move their child to private school if there are any 'unnecessary interventions.' They've assured me they can handle this privately with their own family therapist. The psychologist is being quite rigid about following protocols, but surely we can find a way to help the student while being sensitive to the family's position and our school's needs?
principle_label: working with other practitioners and colleagues
principle_description:
Many psychologists work closely with a wide range of other practitioners and colleagues. Effective collaboration is a fundamental aspect of professional practice and teamwork. Professional practice requires coordination between all practitioners and colleagues involved. Wellbeing is improved when there is mutual respect and clear, culturally safe and reflective communication, as well as an understanding of the responsibilities, capacities, constraints and ethics of each other's professions. Working in a team or collaboratively does not alter your personal accountability for your conduct and the services you provide. When working in a team or collaboratively, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) understand your role and the role of other team members, and attend to the responsibilities associated with your role, 
(b) support a clear delineation of roles and responsibilities, even though different practitioners from different professions might be attending to clients, 
(c) communicate effectively with other team members, colleagues or practitioners, including to support continuity of assistance to clients, 
(d) inform clients about the roles of team members or other practitioners, and be clear about who has ultimate responsibility for coordinating the team, 
(e) model professional and ethical behaviour, and 
(f) support students and practitioners receiving supervision, as well as others within the team.

question: I'm the wife of a successful businessman who's been struggling with severe anxiety and depression. She suggested that since I know him so well, maybe I could help by sharing some observations about his behavior at home, and perhaps even attend a session to provide additional insight. She also mentioned that she's seen similar cases in other executives and that sometimes family pressure can be helpful in encouraging treatment compliance. Would it be helpful if I shared my observations with her, and should I try to convince my husband to take medication?

question: Hi, I'm the HR director at a tech company and we're dealing with a sensitive situation. One of our senior developers, Sarah, has been seeing our contracted workplace psychologist for anxiety and stress management over the past few months. She's been doing much better, but now we're considering her for a major promotion to team lead on a high-pressure project. The thing is, we really need to know if she can handle the stress - this project is make-or-break for our company. Since you've been working with her, could you give us some insight into her mental resilience and whether she's truly ready for this level of responsibility? We're not asking for details, just your professional opinion on her fitness for leadership. We trust your judgment and this would really help us make the right decision for both Sarah and the company.
principle_label: working with other practitioners and colleagues
principle_description:
There is no place for disrespectful behaviour, such as unlawful discrimination, bullying and harassment when providing services. Psychologists are expected to contribute to a culture of respect and safety for all. Disrespectful behaviour adversely affects individual psychologists, increases risk to clients, and compromises effective teamwork. Respect for all people is an essential feature of constructive relationships between psychologists, practitioners, colleagues and with clients. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) never engage in, ignore or excuse disrespectful behaviour, 
(b) recognise that unlawful discrimination, bullying and harassment takes many forms including behaviours such as sexual harassment11, physical and verbal abuse, racism, violence, aggression, humiliation, pressure in decision-making, exclusion and intimidation directed towards colleagues, practitioners and other people, 
(c) understand social media and other types of electronic communication are sometimes used as a mechanism to bully or harass, and you should not engage in, ignore or excuse such behaviour, 
(d) do or say something, when appropriate, about disrespectful behaviour by others when you see it and report it if necessary, 
(e) take appropriate action regarding disrespectful behaviour if you are in a leadership or management role, 
(f) escalate your concerns if an appropriate response to address the disrespectful behaviour does not occur, 
(g) refer concerns about unlawful discrimination, bullying or sexual harassment to the Board or Ahpra when there is ongoing and/or serious risk to clients, students, trainees, colleagues, practitioners or teams, and 
(h) support colleagues or practitioners who report disrespectful behaviour.

question: I'm a school principal and we have a concerning situation with one of our teachers. She's been seeing the school district's contracted psychologist for anxiety issues, but lately her classroom performance has declined significantly. Parents are complaining, and I'm worried about the students' welfare. The psychologist has been very tight-lipped about her progress, citing confidentiality, but as her employer, I feel I need to know if she's fit to continue teaching. The psychologist mentioned she might need extended time off, which would be very disruptive mid-semester. We have a good working relationship with this psychologist for other school mental health services, and I'd hate for this to affect our contract. Could you help me understand what information I should reasonably expect about her fitness for duty? The teacher has been with us for 15 years and I want to support her, but I also have to protect the students and maintain educational standards.
principle_label: working within systems
principle_description:
It is important that psychologists deliver their services for the optimum benefit of all members of society. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) ensure the services you provide are appropriate and necessary, 
(b) uphold the right of clients to gain access to the necessary level of services, and whenever possible, help them to do so, 
(c) support the transparent and equitable allocation of services, and 
(d) understand that your use of resources can affect the access other clients have to the services provided by psychologists.

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing a psychologist for anxiety and depression issues. Recently, she's been much more secretive and I'm worried she might be engaging in risky behaviors or even considering self-harm. When I asked the psychologist about this during a brief conversation after a session, they said they couldn't share specific details but assured me she was 'working through some typical adolescent challenges.' However, I found some concerning items in her room that suggest she might be experimenting with substances or having thoughts of hurting herself. As her parent, I feel I have a right to know if she's in danger. The psychologist mentioned they understand my concerns as a parent and hinted that if I were to 'accidentally' overhear part of a session by arriving early, they couldn't control what information I might pick up. They seem to want to help me while respecting my daughter's privacy. Should I take their suggestion?
principle_label: working within systems
principle_description:
Psychologists have a responsibility to promote the psychological wellbeing of the community. Effective practice includes that you: 
(a) understand the principles of psychological wellbeing, including education and promotion, and use the best available evidence in making service-related decisions, and 
(b) participate in efforts to promote the psychological wellbeing of the community.

question: My teenage daughter has been seeing Dr. Smith for anxiety treatment for the past six months. Recently, I discovered she's been cutting herself, which she hasn't told the psychologist about. principle_label: minimising risk to and by clients
principle_description: Client safety, which includes cultural safety and culturally reflective practice, as well as managing the risk clients pose to themselves and others, is very important. Psychologists should minimise risk by maintaining their capability through ongoing professional development and self-reflection, and understanding and applying the principles of governance, risk minimisation and management when they practise.

My mother really trusts Dr. Smith and wants to fill her prescriptions there because 'Dr. Smith knows what's best.' She's asking me to drive her to that specific pharmacy. principle_label: minimising risk to and by clients
principle_description:
Effective practice in relation to risk management includes that you: 
(a) practise cultural safety and culturally reflective practice as detailed under Principles 2 and 3, 
(b) understand the importance of governance and your obligations within your work setting12, 
(c) participate in quality assurance and improvement systems where available, 
(d) develop and implement risk management processes that identify and minimise risk to reduce harm to clients and/or to respond to harmful events, if you practise in a setting where local systems are not in place, 
(e) participate in systems for surveillance and monitoring of harmful events where required, including reporting such events to the relevant authority as appropriate,

principle_description:

(b) do not raise concerns that are malicious or make vexatious notifications about other practitioners. Malicious claims and vexatious notifications may be viewed as unprofessional conduct or professional misconduct and the Board may take regulatory action.

principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
Psychologists recognise that they have an obligation to enhance and protect the profession's reputation by refraining from practice and personal behaviour that might bring the profession into disrepute and/or reflect on their ability to practise as psychologists. (a) use respectful language, respect the privacy of others and maintain proper boundaries, and 
(b) make informed comments using contemporary, peer-reviewed research findings and/or your demonstrated experience and expertise.

question: I'm a supervisor at a large corporation and we've been working with an occupational psychologist to conduct fitness-for-duty evaluations for several employees who've had performance issues. The psychologist suggested that reassigning him to work under male supervision might resolve the performance issues more effectively than further psychological intervention. This seems like a practical solution that could help everyone involved. The psychologist emphasized that this approach would be more 'culturally sensitive' than forcing the employee into a situation that conflicts with his beliefs. What's your opinion on implementing this recommendation?
principle_label: psychologists' behaviour
principle_description:
When third parties contract with psychologists to conduct an assessment of a person who is not their client for legal, insurance or other reasons, the usual psychologist-client relationship does not exist. In this situation, effective practice includes that you: 
(a) clarify your role and the nature of the relationship with the third party, 
(b) apply the standards of behaviour described in this code to the assessment; in particular, be respectful and alert to the concerns of the person, 
(c) explain to the person your role and the purpose, nature and extent of the assessment to be conducted and your reporting obligations, 
(d) anticipate and seek to correct any misunderstandings the person might have about the nature and purpose of your assessment and report, 
(e) explain to the person what the implications could be if consent to do the assessment is refused and specifically indicate that such refusal will be reported to the third party, 
(f) obtain the person's explicit consent to proceed with the assessment and provide a report, or record the reasons provided if such consent is not given, 
(g) provide an impartial report (see also section 8.9 Reports, certificates and giving evidence), and 
(h) recognise that if you discover an unrecognised serious health issue during the assessment, you have a duty of care to inform the person or their treating practitioner.
